brief.head: The selector’s eye
brief.text: Finance is a cricket se­lec­tor, Ajay Shah said: Main Street of­fers many rival bets, from elec­tric ve­hi­cles to head­phones, and fi­nance picks the ones that will de­liver. {021-C03}

brief.head: Easy in hindsight
brief.text: In the early in­ter­net, no­body knew whether a stock was worth 10x or 10,000x. “It’s very easy to poo poo these things with the ben­e­fit of hind­sight,” Shah said. {021-C11}

brief.head: Chai and credit
brief.text: Bank man­agers once lent over chai to peo­ple they knew, and dis­crim­i­nated against women, Muslims and lower-caste peo­ple. Credit bu­reaus and de­fault mod­els now lend cheaply to strangers. {021-C14}

brief.head: Above the API
brief.text: An al­go­rithm is a human’s trad­ing rule; code is just the clerk. “Human be­ings should com­pose sym­phonies,” Shah said, not do cler­i­cal work below the API. {021-C16}

brief.head: Wall Street’s orders
brief.text: Behind the chairs and cof­fee shops we ad­mire, Shah said, fi­nance pro­cesses in­for­ma­tion and sends out the in­cen­tives: Wall Street tells Main Street what to do. {021-C02}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s tour of finance, from pepper ships to code
lead.head: How pepper built the stock market

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 21

body: Amit Varma once told some­one that Ajay Shah was a lot of fun. Asked what Shah was good at, he said: “Finance.” The reply came back: “Finance and fun? What are you talk­ing about?”
Varma asked Shah for a primer on what fi­nance is, how it evolved, what it does “and how we are not all evil”.

Shah’s an­swer was a his­tory. Each layer of mod­ern fi­nance, he said, solved a felt need of its time, and none of it was de­signed in ad­vance. “That palimpsest of lay­ered so­lu­tions is how we ended up in the mod­ern fi­nance of today.” {021-C01}
## From pep­per to prices
The tour began a thou­sand years ago, with money lent only to peo­ple you knew, un­lim­ited li­a­bil­ity and debtors’ pris­ons.
Then came pep­per. Europe needed spices to pre­serve the meat it stored for win­ter, so it had to send ships to India, and many never re­turned. {021-S01}

No one could af­ford such a bet alone. So came the joint stock com­pany, which spread the risk across thou­sands of small in­vestors, and lim­ited li­a­bil­ity, which capped each one’s loss at what they put in.
The two, Shah said, are in­ti­mately con­nected.

Trading fol­lowed. Cut a com­pany into iden­ti­cal shares and an owner can re­li­ably sell to­mor­row, and the mar­ket pro­duces a price that ev­ery­one can see for next to noth­ing. “This price is a pub­lic good,” Shah said. “It’s an in­for­ma­tion sys­tem, it’s a sta­tis­ti­cal sys­tem.” {021-C08}
That price tells en­trepreneurs where to build and where to stay away. Short sell­ing lets the bears have their say, and every trade, Shah ar­gued, is vol­un­tary and leaves both sides pleased.
## The mod­ern ma­chine
Banks came next: mag­i­cal, Shah said, but frag­ile at the core. Every bank­ing sys­tem goes through a cri­sis every 20 or 30 years.

After 1947 came three pil­lars: telecom­mu­ni­ca­tions, com­pu­ta­tion and the knowl­edge built by aca­demic econ­o­mists. Together they pro­duced credit mod­els, de­riv­a­tives and al­go­rith­mic trad­ing, where code does a clerk’s job.

Running through the tour was a lament for India. Regulators fret when shares go to zero, and pop­ulists chase rich pro­mot­ers for a company’s debts. “I find it strik­ing that 17th cen­tury busi­ness and com­mer­cial con­cepts in the UK in many ways are miss­ing in India today,” Shah said.

Finance can go wrong in two ways, he said. A so­ci­ety can sti­fle it, which is largely where India is, or leave it to pure lais­sez-faire and ig­nore real mar­ket fail­ures. “So you can ban fi­nance, that doesn’t work. Or if you just do pure lais­sez-faire, that doesn’t work ei­ther.” {021-C17}
## The long di­ver­gence
Varma then turned to the Middle East, through the work of Timur Kuran. Around 1000 AD, its econ­omy re­sem­bled Europe’s. Then it stag­nated, while Europe zoomed ahead.

The cul­prits, in Kuran’s ac­count, were laws that were fairer than Europe’s. Islamic in­her­i­tance gave daugh­ters a share and scat­tered a dead partner’s stake among many heirs, so part­ner­ships stayed small and short, and joint stock com­pa­nies never formed. {021-C19}
Varma saw no recipe in it, only a les­son in how “these lit­tle ac­ci­dents of his­tory” can lead to path de­pen­dence.
Shah brought the story home. India, he warned, has the word “com­pany” with­out all of its sub­stance, and this fail­ure of in­sti­tu­tion build­ing could hold the coun­try back.

second.label: Dead capital
second.head: Charity on a dead road
second.deck: Amit Varma, via Timur Kuran, on endowments that outlived their purpose

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the waqf that funded a caravanserai

body: A waqf, Amit Varma said, was a mar­vel­lous in­no­va­tion: a rich man’s en­dow­ment for a fixed pub­lic pur­pose, for­ever. He called it “the vol­un­tary pri­vate pro­vi­sion of pub­lic goods”, with no co­er­cion and no tax­a­tion. {021-C20}

But the pur­pose could never change. Timur Kuran’s ex­am­ple is a car­a­vanserai, a road­side inn, founded on the Silk Route in the mid-1200s. By the 1600s no­body used the route, yet the money could not be moved: it was what Hernando de Soto would call dead cap­i­tal, Varma said. {021-S07}
Another waqf built water foun­tains, thirty a year. {#thirty} Once piped water spread, the need was for bet­ter pipes, but the funds were tied to foun­tains.

quote.text: But you’re not al­lowed to shift the funds out of the car­a­vanserai, right? So they are kind of stuck there.

third.head: Small town, first class

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the satellite that came like a railway

body: Ravi Narayan, one of the found­ing team of NSE, had a line that Ajay Shah called beau­ti­ful: when satel­lite com­mu­ni­ca­tions for NSE trad­ing first reached a small town in India, it was like a rail­way line ar­riv­ing there for the first time. {021-S05}
Before that, an in­vestor in such a town had to place long-distance trunk calls to a Bombay bro­ker. Then, Shah said, “Suddenly ev­ery­body was an equal first class par­tic­i­pant.”

NSE, he said, was a global pi­o­neer in elec­tronic trad­ing over satel­lite. Telecommunications was the first of the three pil­lars of mod­ern fi­nance, he said, since fi­nance is “the busi­ness of bits and bytes”. {021-C13}
Today peo­ple trade on a mo­bile phone, he noted, which would have seemed mirac­u­lous only a short while ago.

box.title: A masterpiece, mid-episode
box.text: Amit Varma paused mid-episode to rec­om­mend Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, a mas­ter­piece, he said, and per­haps the most im­por­tant essay of the last cen­tury: prices carry in­for­ma­tion that no cen­tral plan­ner can ever gather. {021-R03}

sections.label: The first layer
sections.head: When my ship comes in
sections.caption: the ship that might not come in
body: A thou­sand years ago, Ajay Shah said, fi­nance was sim­ple: money lent to peo­ple you knew, with un­lim­ited li­a­bil­ity. If you failed, the lenders came after your house, and if that was not enough, you went to debtors’ prison.

Fitting out a ship for India was a vast ex­pense in a Europe that was not yet rich, and about one ship in four was lost to cy­clones, pi­rates or some­thing else. Hence the English phrase “when my ship comes in”. {021-S02}
## Two in­ven­tions, one idea
The first an­swer was the joint stock com­pany. Instead of five peo­ple pool­ing money, thou­sands could, each plac­ing a bet they could af­ford to lose. {021-C04}

The sec­ond was lim­ited li­a­bil­ity. If the com­pany failed, lenders got “the car­cass of the com­pany” and could not chase the share­hold­ers. Without that cap, Shah said, you can­not at­tract thou­sands of in­vestors; the two ideas go to­gether.
Amit Varma ar­gued that it helps lenders too: more ships mean bet­ter ship­build­ing, economies of scale and more bright minds.

In India, Shah said, these ideas have not yet sunk in. Regulators get un­happy when a share goes to zero, and pop­ulists want pro­mot­ers to pay a failed company’s debts. “If you’re not miss­ing any flights, you’re going too early,” he said. {021-C05}
~ Separating money from ideas quick­ened cap­i­tal­ism, he added. The econ­o­mist John Hicks said the Industrial Revolution was as much about the stock mar­ket as the steam en­gine. {021-J11}

quote.text: Because if your ship came in, you were very rich. But there was a very high chance that your ship would not come in.

sections.label: The second layer
sections.head: Bulls, bears and free speech
sections.caption: the price as a public good
body: Once there were many share­hold­ers, Ajay Shah said, the next step was nat­u­ral: “Can I not sell them to you?” So trad­ing began, bring­ing two pieces of magic.

The first was liq­uid­ity. No two flats are alike, and sell­ing gold means hag­gling over pu­rity. Cut Infosys into a bil­lion iden­ti­cal shares and an owner can sell to­mor­row. “It was a rev­o­lu­tion in world his­tory,” Shah said. {021-C07}

The sec­ond was a pub­lic price. When soft­ware com­pa­nies are val­ued highly, it beck­ons en­trepreneurs to build an­other; when an in­dus­try trades poorly, the mar­ket shouts at them to stay away. {021-C08}
## The right to dis­agree

If you think a share is over­priced but do not own it, you can bor­row it, sell it and buy it back later. Short sell­ing, Shah said, is a kind of free­dom of speech: you can say a se­cu­rity is too cheap, or too dear. {021-C09}

Every such trade is vol­un­tary, and each side thinks it got the bet­ter deal. Short sell­ing adds more of these dou­ble thank-you mo­ments, since the long-term holder earns a rental fee for lend­ing the share. {021-C10}
Amit Varma said that blam­ing short sell­ers when things go wrong is shoot­ing the mes­sen­ger.
~ He likened mar­kets to chess, which the player Levon Aronian called a con­ver­sa­tion. The mar­ket, Varma said, is “a sym­phony of voices ex­press­ing opin­ions”.

quote.text: It is a vol­un­tary trans­ac­tion be­tween con­sent­ing adults, and there’s a dou­ble thank you mo­ment there.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the price as a public good

sections.label: The third layer
sections.head: Side bets on the main bets
sections.caption: the three pillars of modern finance
body: Banks, Ajay Shah said, are mag­i­cal and frag­ile at once. With heavy lever­age they cre­ate, out of thin air, an il­lu­sion of liq­uid­ity and of fund­ing long-dated as­sets with short-dated de­posits. He quoted the econ­o­mist Merton Miller, who called bank­ing “a dis­as­ter-prone 19th cen­tury in­dus­try”. {021-C12}
Because politi­cians will not let grand­moth­ers and den­tists lose their money, bank­ing turns po­lit­i­cal. Shah is not op­ti­mistic that the prob­lem can be solved.
## Three pil­lars

After 1947 the mir­a­cles began. Telecommunications con­nected mar­kets, com­pu­ta­tion took over book­keep­ing and cal­cu­la­tion, and aca­demic eco­nom­ics sup­plied knowl­edge about port­fo­lios, risk and di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion. {021-C13}
The great­est flow­er­ing, Shah said, was de­riv­a­tives, “a sys­tem of side bets on the main bets”, which let peo­ple with knowl­edge but lit­tle cap­i­tal join in price dis­cov­ery. {021-C15}

They are not new. Shah re­called a speech at the Bombay Stock Exchange about the late 19th cen­tury, which said the na­tives were “as good as any­body in the world on trad­ing in put and call op­tions”. {021-S06}
~ Algorithmic trad­ing, he said, sim­ply hands a human’s rule to a tire­less clerk in code. “It won’t take a break to have chai, it won’t have a bad hair day.” {021-J09}

quote.text: We got tech­nolo­gies of com­mu­ni­ca­tion, we got tech­nolo­gies of com­pu­ta­tion, and we got great ex­plo­sions of human knowl­edge.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the three pillars of modern finance

sections.label: The detour
sections.head: Too fair to get rich
sections.caption: the Middle East’s long divergence
body: Around 1000 AD, Amit Varma said, the Middle East’s econ­omy was very sim­i­lar to Europe’s. Then it stag­nated until the mid­dle of the 19th cen­tury, while Europe zoomed ahead. {021-C18}

Timur Kuran, who once taught Ajay Shah, de­mol­ishes three usual ex­pla­na­tions. Islam was not hos­tile to com­merce: Muslim traders dom­i­nated trad­ing hubs. The re­gion did in­no­vate, in gov­ern­ment in­sti­tu­tions and tax­a­tion. And it was not in­cu­ri­ous, as the his­to­rian Bernard Lewis ar­gued: it kept up with mil­i­tary text­books, but never took up eco­nomic ones.
## The irony of fair­ness

Islamic in­her­i­tance law was more eq­ui­table than pri­mo­gen­i­ture in Northern Europe, where the el­dest son got ev­ery­thing. Two-thirds went to the ex­tended fam­ily and the rest to sons and daugh­ters, a daugh­ter get­ting half a son’s share. {#twothirds}

But when a part­ner died, his share was spread among many heirs. So part­ner­ships stayed small and brief, joint stock com­pa­nies never formed, and nor did the laws and ac­count­ing that grow around them. Europe’s rule was, in Varma’s words, a “shitty law, com­pletely un­fair, but at least you know that there is a suc­ces­sor”. {021-C19}
~ Varma drew no pre­scrip­tive les­son, he said, only an ap­pre­ci­a­tion of the com­plex­ity of the world.

quote.text: Now the cen­tral ques­tion of The Long Divergence is that circa a thou­sand AD, the Middle East eco­nom­i­cally was very sim­i­lar to Europe.

portraits.caption: Timur Kuran
portraits.credit: CharlesArthurMiller at English Wikipedia, public domain

quote.text: The role in shap­ing re­source al­lo­ca­tion in the real econ­omy and in shap­ing prices in the fi­nan­cial econ­omy should go to the peo­ple with the knowl­edge and not the peo­ple who have in­her­ited fam­ily wealth.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Pepper, pigeons, a burning factory and a decade among the Pathans

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah answers a puzzle from his childhood
stories.head: A matter of life and pepper
body: As a child, Ajay Shah never un­der­stood why Europeans would board a ship with a 25 per cent chance of dying on every voy­age, just to get pep­per. “I could just have salt on my omelette,” he said.

The an­swer, he said, was the win­ter. Europe’s pop­u­la­tion had grown to the limit of what its farms could carry, and the only way to sur­vive the cold months was to store meat from the sum­mer. {021-S01}

And meat rots. “So you had ex­actly two choices,” Shah said. “You would ei­ther eat rot­ten meat, which is sub­jec­tively not a pleas­ant ex­pe­ri­ence, and you would then suf­fer dis­ease and die. Or you could have spices in order to pre­serve the meat.”

Then, in 1453, the Ottoman Empire con­quered Istanbul and cut off the land route for spices from Asia, above all India. {#istanbul} Europe now had to find a sea route, and the great age of ex­plo­ration began.

The Portuguese worked their way, as Shah put it, al­most to the edge of South America, back down the Cape of Good Hope and up to Madagascar. There, “lo and be­hold”, they landed on a Malay who knew how to ride the mon­soon cur­rents to Calicut.
That was the start of the spice trade, and of a fi­nan­cial puz­zle. A ship that came home made its back­ers very rich; one lost to a cy­clone or pi­rates paid them noth­ing. {021-S02}
~ In a Europe that was not yet rich, no one per­son could stake that much on a sin­gle voy­age. From that pres­sure, Shah said, came the first great fi­nan­cial in­no­va­tions.
stories.why: Behaviour that looks ir­ra­tional from out­side often an­swers a life-or-death con­straint. Rebuild the prob­lem peo­ple faced, Shah’s method says, and his­tory makes sense; so does fi­nance, whose in­sti­tu­tions began as an­swers to such real prob­lems. {021-C01}
stories.postscript: Varma’s pro­posed title for a his­tory of the world: *From Pepper to Peppa Pig*. Shah had never heard of Peppa Pig. {021-J03}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on why Europe risked death for pepper

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why getting the news first is no crime
stories.head: News by pigeon post
body: Reuters, Ajay Shah said, made its name with pi­geons. Unsure whether Reuters was then an or­gan­i­sa­tion or a per­son, he told how it was the first to carry news of the Battle of Waterloo back to London, where it could be used for trad­ing. {021-S04}
It was make or break: would Britain win or lose? Fortunes hung on the an­swer, and Reuters got it to a trad­ing venue first.

In India, Shah said, peo­ple would whine that this was un­fair ac­cess to in­for­ma­tion. He saw it dif­fer­ently: “That was the in­no­va­tion, that was their con­tri­bu­tion, that they ac­tu­ally cre­ated a novel path­way to that in­for­ma­tion.”
~ That, he said, is how in­for­ma­tion gets into prices: everyone’s knowl­edge is pooled in a pub­lic price, and any­one who dis­agrees can put their money where their mouth is.
stories.why: A faster chan­nel for news is a con­tri­bu­tion, not cheat­ing: it is how in­for­ma­tion reaches the price. The same logic, Shah ar­gued, de­fends short sell­ers, who let the bear­ish view into the price too. {021-C09}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Reuters and the pigeons of Waterloo

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on news that rushes into prices
stories.head: Smoke signals for the market
body: In the early years of NSE, Ajay Shah wan­dered the coun­try teach­ing. Somewhere near Coimbatore, a man told him a story. {021-S03}

He was rid­ing his two-wheeler past a fac­tory when he saw smoke com­ing out of it: the fac­tory was on fire. His re­sponse: “I hit the gas and I ran to the near­est NSE bro­ker and I sold all my shares in that com­pany.”

Shah called it a funny story, and it shows the price sys­tem at work. Whoever stum­bles on news has a rea­son to push it into the price, and no­body has to order them to. “This is a de­cen­tralised, dis­trib­uted, vol­un­tary in­for­ma­tion sys­tem,” he said. “There’s no co­er­cion.”
~ It is the same ma­chin­ery that, Shah had said ear­lier, makes a share price a pub­lic good: a read­out any­one can con­sult al­most free. {021-C08}

quote.text: Now just see the in­cen­tives for in­for­ma­tion to turn into the price.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the factory on fire

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s recommendation, and a decade in the Frontier
stories.head: The question that kept her up
body: In the late 1980s, Mukulika Banerjee was won­der­ing whether to do a PhD. The ad­vice she got was this: “Only do a PhD if there is a ques­tion that keeps you awake at night.” {021-S08}

Her ques­tion was about the Pathans, stereo­typed as vi­o­lent. How had the non­vi­o­lent Khudai Khidmatgar, led by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the Frontier Gandhi, come out of them? The move­ment was wiped out after Partition.
She spent ten years on the book, trav­el­ling from vil­lage to vil­lage in the North-West Frontier Province in search of el­ders who had once been mem­bers. {#tenyears}
~ Her find­ing, Amit Varma said, was pro­found: the Pathans’ non­vi­o­lence was not im­ported from the West, nor from Gandhi. “They were or­ganic and they emerged from within.”
stories.why: Good schol­ar­ship starts with a ques­tion you can­not let go of, and pa­tient field­work can over­turn a stereo­type. Varma said her book, out around 2001, de­served far wider read­er­ship than it got. {021-R16}
stories.postscript: Served each home’s one prized chicken, she felt guilty, so, de­spite being a Hindu, she began eat­ing beef in­stead. {021-S09}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 21. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Timur Kuran (CharlesArthurMiller at English Wikipedia, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Levon Aronian (Stefan64, CC BY-SA 3.0); Hernando de Soto (Institute for Liberty and Democracy, CC BY-SA 3.0).

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s eco­nomic his­tory of Indian fi­nance from 1947 to today, which Amit calls close to mag­is­te­rial and the de­fin­i­tive work on the sub­ject.

shelf.title: Capital Ideas
shelf.creator: Peter L Bernstein
shelf.why: A lovely, if slightly dated, story of how the ideas of mod­ern fi­nance emerged once mod­els and com­put­ers came in; Ajay calls it ‘just great fun’.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Double ‘Thank You’ Moment
shelf.creator: John Stossel
shelf.why: Stossel’s sim­plest pic­ture of pos­i­tive-sum ex­change: when you buy a cof­fee, you thank the barista and the barista thanks you, be­cause both are bet­ter off.

shelf.title: The Bankable Wisdom of Harsh Vardhan (Episode 352 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Harsh Vardhan, whom Ajay calls a deep thinker on banks, ar­gues that bank­ing, mag­i­cal and fun­da­men­tally frag­ile, is es­sen­tial to a suc­cess­ful cap­i­tal­ism.

shelf.title: Looking beyond the label ‘algorithmic trading’
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Expands his ar­gu­ment that al­go­rithms are human ideas car­ried out by code act­ing as a clerk, and that the hos­til­ity to algo trad­ing comes from ig­no­rance.

shelf.title: When Genius Failed
shelf.creator: Roger Lowenstein
shelf.why: It tells the story of the col­lapse of Long-Term Capital Management, a firm with sev­eral Nobel Prize-winning aca­demics.

shelf.title: Inventing Money
shelf.creator: Nicholas Dunbar
shelf.why: Ajay thinks Dunbar’s LTCM book, which came out a year later, is the bet­ter of the two.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Private Truths, Public Lies
shelf.creator: Timur Kuran
shelf.why: Kuran’s the­ory of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and pref­er­ence cas­cades: regimes look unan­i­mously sup­ported until peo­ple dis­cover that oth­ers se­cretly dis­agree too.

shelf.title: The Long Divergence
shelf.creator: Timur Kuran
shelf.why: It knocks down the usual ex­pla­na­tions for the Middle East’s eco­nomic stag­na­tion and shows how in­her­i­tance law and the waqf held it back.

shelf.title: Freedoms Delayed
shelf.creator: Timur Kuran
shelf.why: It fol­lows the same in­sti­tu­tional story into its po­lit­i­cal con­se­quences and is rich in his­tory.

shelf.title: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (Episode 349 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The long ver­sion of Timur Kuran’s ideas, from pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and the Soviet col­lapse to the long di­ver­gence.

shelf.title: Halfway From Coal, Halfway to Diamond (Episode 1)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The start­ing point of the Kuran con­nec­tion and the hosts’ ear­lier dis­cus­sion of his ideas.

shelf.title: The Mystery of Capital
shelf.creator: Hernando De Soto
shelf.why: De Soto’s idea of ‘dead capital’: with­out prop­erty rights, un­ti­tled slum homes and re­stricted land are worth some­thing but can’t be bor­rowed against or in­vested, so the poor can’t turn what they own into cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: The Pathan Unarmed
shelf.creator: Mukulika Banerjee
shelf.why: Ten years of field­work on how Pathan peas­ants, stereo­typed as vi­o­lent, built the subcontinent’s great­est non­vi­o­lent move­ment, the Khudai Khidmatgar: Bacha Khan rooted it in the inner jihad and the Pashtun codes of courage, hos­pi­tal­ity and refuge.

shelf.title: The Incredible Curiosities of Mukulika Banerjee (Episode 276 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Mukulika Banerjee’s re­search sto­ries: her fight for fund­ing and her field­work in the North-West Frontier Province hunt­ing for sur­viv­ing Khudai Khidmatgars, which Amit calls a clas­sic quest nar­ra­tive.

shelf.title: Peppa Pig
shelf.why: Amit’s tongue-in-cheek prom­ise to in­tro­duce Ajay to ‘that magic’.

laughs.text: Amit’s opener: some­one asked what Ajay is good at, Amit said ‘Finance,’ and they replied ‘Finance and fun? What are you talk­ing about?’ Amit says his de­fence of fi­nance as fun ‘was at­trib­uted to bias.’
Ajay: ‘eco­nom­ics is the sec­ond most im­por­tant thing in the world.’ Amit: ‘Wait, wait, wait. What is first? This is a fam­ily show.’

Amit: ‘If a his­tory of the world is writ­ten, it could eas­ily be called From Pepper to Peppa Pig.’ Ajay has never heard of Peppa Pig, and Amit prom­ises to send links ‘and in­tro­duce you to that magic.’
After in­vok­ing Mahalanobis’s phrase ‘com­mand­ing heights of the economy’ for fi­nance, Ajay adds that Mahalanobis ‘would, of course, turn in his metaphor­i­cal grave when it was put like this.’
Amit on cen­tral plan­ners ‘like Prashant-da’: ‘never say any­thing against Bengalis un­less they are plan­ners.’
Ajay calls Amit a ‘ge­nius poker intellectual’ in his al­go­rith­mic trad­ing ex­am­ple. Amit says he ‘started purring peacefully’ at being called a GPI, which ‘fills my heart with glad­ness.’
Ajay on the AI as a clerk: ‘It won’t take a break to have chai, it won’t have a bad hair day, it will be mil­lisec­ond, split sec­ond, pre­ci­sion.’
‘Wall Street tells Main Street what to do’, the fa­mous line Ajay uses to frame fi­nance as the brain that guides the real econ­omy.
John Hicks: the Industrial Revolution ‘was as much about the stock mar­ket as it was about the steam engine’, the in­vis­i­ble ma­chine along­side James Watt’s vis­i­ble one.
Merton Miller’s de­scrip­tion of bank­ing as ‘a dis­as­ter-prone 19th cen­tury in­dus­try.’
Chess player Levon Aronian called a chess game a con­ver­sa­tion. Amit ap­plies this to mar­kets as ‘a sym­phony of voices ex­press­ing opin­ions.’
